description: We built ARIADNE for the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge: a Mars EVA planner that plans, rehearses and guards a two-astronaut walk through the boxwork ridges of Mount Sharp in Gale crater, using NASA and USGS terrain, Curiosity rover data and space-weather records.
summary: ARIADNE plans, rehearses and guards a two-astronaut walk on Mars, using the boxwork ridges of Mount Sharp, which Curiosity explored in 2025–26, as the test site. From NASA and USGS terrain models, orbital images and Curiosity's own positions, it maps where a suited walker can go, how much open sky each spot sees (a guide to radiation shielding), and which ridge, wall and hollow stops would teach the most. It then plans three walks, Safest, Balanced and Most science, that never break the "thread": at every point the crew keeps enough air to walk back to the rover with a reserve. The crew can rehearse the walk in 3D past real Curiosity photos, then follow it on a visor display that never shows more than four things at once, a glove-sized cuff tablet that works offline, and a one-page printed cuff card. A replay of the May 20, 2024 solar storm shows why it matters: Earth was 15.8 light-minutes away and the particles reached Mars in tens of minutes, so the crew must act on their own alarm, and ARIADNE sends both walkers to the lowest-dose refuge. Every number is labeled measured, derived, modeled or placeholder, and a Validation tab shows every check, including the one that failed.
details:
What it does. ARIADNE is a planning, rehearsal and guidance system for a Mars EVA (a walk outside), built for the boxwork ridges on Mount Sharp in Gale crater. It answers the questions a crew and its planners would ask before and during a walk: where can we safely go, what is worth sampling, what route keeps us safe, and what do we do if a solar storm hits while we are out?

How it works. A Python pipeline runs at build time and a static web app shows the results; there is no server and no secret key.

Data. The pipeline crops the USGS 1 m elevation model and 25 cm image mosaic of Gale crater (built from HiRISE, CTX and HRSC), the MOLA global elevation model, Curiosity's 2,893 positions in the boxwork from PLACES, ChemCam targets, the four boxwork drill holes and THEMIS night-infrared images, and records where each file came from.

Layers. From those it builds slope at each traveller's footprint, walkability for a suited walker and for the rover, terrain horizons in 72 directions out to 100 km, a sky-shielding index calibrated on Curiosity's radiation measurement beside the Murray Buttes in 2016 (the model reproduces the measured 3.8% dose drop with one parameter and gets the blocked sky to 18.5% against the paper's 19%), line of sight from the rover's antenna, sunlight, boxwork ridges and fractures, a science score for ridge, wall and hollow transects, and a confidence map.

Routes. A 16-neighbour route graph prices every step by time, effort, caution, radiation and uncertainty, using a published walking-cost model with placeholder suit settings. OR-Tools picks whole transects within a 6-hour walk. The rover acts as a mobile radio relay and as the shelter: every point of every plan stays within a set walking time of the rover, wherever it is parked or driving. Every plan is checked at least every 5 m for the thread (air to get back with a reserve), the buddy rule, the walk to the rover, and radio shadows; the thread holds in 1,000 of 1,000 random scenarios.

The app. The Habitat Planner shows the map with each layer's source, the three plans side by side with a "price of safety" line (Safest gives up 43% of the science value and gains 76 minutes of margin against Most science), a timeline, an assumptions panel, and a 3D rehearsal with Curiosity Navcam photos placed where they were taken. The Visor HUD overlays the first-person view with at most four elements in white and cyan, each with its own shape, checked against simulated colour blindness. The Cuff Tablet has 64-pixel controls, a "what you'll see" photo for each station, the four station steps, and a sample log that works offline. The printed cuff card fits one page with abort routes to the rover.

Storm replay. The May 20, 2024 event (a far-side eruption DONKI logs at 05:22 UTC; JPL reports that an astronaut beside Curiosity would have received 8,100 micrograys) starts in the middle of the walk. The alert comes on cue, storm mode takes over, and both walkers head for the rover; the panel sets RAD's figure beside modeled doses with and without the rover.

Benefits. It turns ten kinds of open NASA data into one meter-scale plan a crew can rehearse and follow, with the safety rules enforced by the planner rather than left to memory. It is honest about uncertainty: the rover-walkability check failed in the boxwork (79.8% of Curiosity's positions classed passable against a 95% target) because the ridges sit at the elevation model's resolution limit, so the planner stays conservative and the surfaces mark ground where the map may be over-cautious. The same pipeline built the Murray Buttes site, where that check passes (99.8%).

What we hope to achieve. A planning concept that future crews, mission planners and students can pick up and test: any HiRISE terrain model could become a site, and the suit and walking settings, now placeholders, could be replaced by measured values for a real Mars suit.

Tools. Python (NumPy, SciPy, scikit-image, rasterio, pyproj, numba, OR-Tools), TypeScript with React, deck.gl and three.js, Vitest, Playwright and axe-core for tests, GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages. Code licensed Apache-2.0. Source: https://github.com/vyom-aggarwal/ARIADNE

Use of SI (Super Intelligence). Claude researched sources, reviewed each phase and proposed most of the decisions we approved or rejected. Claude Code wrote the pipeline and web app code, ran the data processing, tests and checks, and drafted the documents. Our team chose the challenge, directed the work, approved or rejected each decision, got clearance from our Local Lead, and is responsible for the submission. Every source file and every commit since the kickoff carries an SI note, the packaged data records it in its metadata, and the app's footer says so. No images, video or audio were generated by SI; all imagery is real NASA mission imagery with its credit. Full account: https://github.com/vyom-aggarwal/ARIADNE/blob/main/AI_USE.md
